Economists measure economic growth by constructing real GDP, which eliminates the effect of price changes. Real GDP is the sum of the quantities of final goods produced in a given period times constant (rather than current) prices. This allows them to focus on the change in the quantity of goods produced, rather than changes in prices. For example, in an economy that only produces cars, real GDP would use the price of cars in a given year to multiply the quantity of cars produced in each year, providing a measure of growth in car production without price changes affecting the measure.

Mortgage-backed securities played a significant role in the financial crisis. Banks and other financial institutions bundled mortgages into new securities and sold them to other banks and investors. These securities were often repackaged into yet new securities, making it difficult to assess their value. The decline in housing prices led to many borrowers defaulting on their mortgages, as the value of their mortgage often exceeded the price of the house. This complexity and opacity turned a housing price decline into a major financial crisis, which few economists had anticipated. The crisis quickly spread to other countries through trade and financial channels, leading to a global recession.
